text: Lexical retrieval matches query terms against indexed document terms. BM25 uses term frequency, inverse document frequency, and document length normalization to rank candidate documents.
Dense retrieval represents documents and queries as embedding vectors. A semantic search can retrieve relevant text even when the query uses different words from the document.
A vector store keeps embedding vectors together with document identifiers and metadata. Similarity search compares a query vector with stored vectors and returns the nearest candidates.
Graph retrieval focuses on entities and their relationships. A graph may connect machine learning to neural networks, neural networks to computer vision, and computer vision to satellite imagery.
Hybrid retrieval combines multiple candidate sources. A search system can combine BM25 keyword matches, dense semantic matches, and graph-based matches before producing a unified candidate set.

Reciprocal Rank Fusion, or RRF, merges ranked result lists using the rank position assigned by each retriever. It does not require raw BM25 and vector similarity scores to share the same numerical scale.

Cross-encoder reranking scores a query and candidate document together. Retrieval first produces a manageable candidate set, and the cross-encoder then performs a more detailed relevance assessment on those candidates.
Retrieval-augmented generation uses retrieved evidence as context for a language model. The generator receives the selected source text and produces an answer grounded in that supplied context.

A query planner can inspect a query before retrieval and choose an execution strategy. Identifier-heavy queries may benefit from lexical search, explanatory questions may benefit from dense retrieval, relationship questions may benefit from graph retrieval, and complex queries may use hybrid retrieval.

An inverted index maps terms to the documents that contain those terms. A positional index additionally records token positions, which allows a system to answer phrase queries such as machine learning.

Consider the identifier CVE-2025-1234. Identifier searches often benefit from lexical matching because exact character sequences are important. Semantic similarity can retrieve conceptually related security documents without guaranteeing an exact identifier match.
Suppose a user asks, 'How do models learn patterns from examples?' A dense retriever can identify documents about representation learning or training even if the exact query words are absent.

Suppose a graph contains Machine Learning -> uses -> Neural Networks -> applied_to -> Computer Vision. A relationship query about how machine learning connects to computer vision can use graph traversal to discover the intermediate entities.

A practical retrieval pipeline can first retrieve 50 candidates with BM25, dense search, and graph search, merge them with RRF, rerank the merged candidates with a cross-encoder, and then pass the strongest evidence to a language model.

A grounded answer should preserve provenance. The system should retain the document IDs and source text used to build the final RAG context so that an answer can be traced back to the retrieved evidence.
